finding.claim: Unauthenticated GET /preview passes the raw `url` query parameter to requests.get with no allowlist, scheme check, or redirect re-validation, and returns the first 500 characters of the response body to the caller. An attacker can reach internal services and cloud metadata endpoints.

trace.note: target = request.args.get("url", "") takes the raw query value with no validation
requests.get(target, timeout=5) dispatches the request; no allowlist or IP check between source and sink
requests follows redirects for GET by default, so a 3xx from an attacker-controlled host can redirect the fetch to internal or metadata addresses (redirect risk: yes)
resp.status_code and resp.text[:500] are returned to the caller, so the attacker reads the response (not blind SSRF)

finding.guards_checked: No authentication decorator on the /preview route. No scheme or host allowlist. timeout=5 limits duration only, not destinations. No redirect disabling or re-validation. Triage Step 0 answered (unauthenticated external user; GET /preview?url=<internal or metadata URL>; the request triggers the fetch; reads internal or metadata content). Triage Check 3: no server binding in repo, so ingress is treated as public per SSRF skill default; no Shodan lookup since target host unknown. Not excluded by corpus exclusion (no README or training-app markers). Not a DEPLOY-REC case (app purpose is not user-configured HTTP calls). Validation Tier 0. Other sinks checked and closed: /partner (app.py:22-26) validates urlparse(target).hostname against ALLOWED_HOSTS via strict set membership before requests.get, residual redirect risk only via a compromised allowlisted partner (trusted-service rule); /health (app.py:10, 32) uses a startup environment-variable URL, not user-controlled.

verdict.reason: app.py:15 takes the raw `url` query parameter with no validation, app.py:16 passes it straight to requests.get (which follows GET redirects by default), and app.py:17 returns the first 500 characters of the response body to the caller; the /preview route (app.py:13-17) has no auth, allowlist, or host check, so an unauthenticated attacker can read internal or metadata content. The /partner allowlist at app.py:23-24 is on a different route and does not apply here.
